title: Mobile Client Architecture Patterns
summary: Layering a whole app — presentation, domain, data — and module boundaries, one level above any single screen's MVVM. The architecture questions a mobile system design interview actually probes.

slides.markdown:
MVVM, MVI, and similar patterns answer 'how is one screen structured.' This topic is one level up: how does a **whole app** — dozens or hundreds of screens, shared data, shared business rules — stay maintainable as it grows from a five-screen MVP to a hundred-screen product with twenty engineers touching it concurrently?

The answer is the same shape every mature mobile app converges on: layered responsibilities (presentation, domain, data) and module boundaries that make 'who's allowed to depend on what' an enforceable rule, not a tribal convention that erodes as the team grows.

slides.subTitle: presentation, domain, data
slides.markdown:
Three layers, each with one job and a one-directional dependency rule (each layer depends only on the one below it, never above):

- **Presentation** — UI and view models/state holders. Renders data, forwards user actions. Should contain almost no business logic of its own.
- **Domain** — use cases / business rules, independent of both UI and data source details. "Can this user place an order given their current cart and inventory" lives here, not in a view model or a network client.
- **Data** — repositories that abstract away *where* data actually comes from (network, local database, cache) behind a single interface the domain layer calls.

The test for whether layering is actually working: can you swap the data layer's implementation (mock network responses for testing, swap SQLite for a different local store) without touching domain or presentation code at all? If not, the layers have leaked into each other.

slides.sectionTitle: MVVM vs MVI vs Clean Architecture
slides.subTitle: at the whole-app level
slides.markdown:
| | MVVM | MVI | Clean Architecture |
|---|---|---|---|
| Core idea | View binds to observable state on a ViewModel | Unidirectional: Intent -> reducer -> single immutable State -> View | Strict layering (presentation/domain/data) with dependency inversion |
| State shape | often several independent observable properties | one single State object per screen, always fully replaced | not prescriptive about state shape — a layering rule, not a state pattern |
| Debuggability | good, but scattered state can drift out of sync | excellent — one state snapshot per screen, easy to log/replay | depends on what's layered inside it |
| Common pairing | works well inside any of the three layers below | often paired with Clean Architecture's domain layer | the layering discipline this whole topic teaches |

These aren't mutually exclusive: a real app commonly uses Clean Architecture's layering for the *whole app's* structure, with MVI or MVVM as the specific pattern *inside* the presentation layer for how one screen's state is organized. Presenting them as competing alternatives is a common interview miss — they answer different-scoped questions.

slides.subTitle: why large apps split into independent modules
slides.markdown:
Beyond a certain size, an app split into one giant module (or a handful of loosely-organized ones) starts costing the team real time: every change triggers a full rebuild, every engineer's IDE indexes the entire codebase, and it's easy to accidentally couple two features that shouldn't know about each other because nothing enforces a boundary.

**Feature modules** — a `checkout` module, a `profile` module, a `search` module, each with its own build target — fix this structurally: a change inside `checkout` only rebuilds `checkout` and whatever explicitly depends on it, not the whole app. Just as importantly, a module's public interface is the *only* thing other modules can see — its internals are genuinely private, which is a much stronger boundary than 'please don't import from that package' as an unenforced convention.

slides.subTitle: one source of truth behind repositories
slides.markdown:
A **repository** is the data layer's public interface — the domain layer calls `orderRepository.getOrders()` with no idea whether that hits a network call, a local database, an in-memory cache, or some combination decided by the repository itself.

The repository's real job, beyond just fetching, is establishing **one source of truth**: typically the local database, kept in sync with the network, with the UI always reading from that single local source rather than juggling 'is this the network response or the cached one.' A screen observing the local database directly gets updated automatically the moment a background sync writes fresh data, with no manual 'did the fetch finish, now update the UI' wiring — this pattern is exactly what [Offline-First Design](offline-first-design) builds out in full.

| | Single module | Multi-module |
|---|---|---|
| Build time as app grows | degrades — every change rebuilds everything | scales better — only affected modules rebuild |
| Boundary enforcement | convention only, easy to violate silently | compiler-enforced via module visibility |
| Setup/maintenance overhead | minimal | real — module graph, dependency management across modules |
| Right for | small apps, small teams, early-stage products | larger apps, larger teams, apps expected to grow significantly |

The common mistake is over-modularizing an early-stage app before it needs it — a five-screen MVP with two engineers pays real overhead maintaining a fifteen-module dependency graph for a problem it doesn't have yet. The other common mistake is under-modularizing too long — waiting until build times are already painful and dozens of accidental cross-feature couplings have calcified makes the eventual split far more expensive than doing it incrementally, earlier, as clear feature boundaries emerge.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a God repository every feature depends on
slides.markdown:
A common architecture-decay pattern: one `AppRepository` (or `DataManager`, `ApiService`) that every feature module imports and that accumulates methods for every feature's data needs over time, because it's the path of least resistance for whoever's adding the next feature.

The result is a single class no one fully understands, that changes constantly (so it's always mid-review by someone), and that couples every feature to every other feature transitively through this one shared dependency — modularizing the rest of the app buys nothing if every module still funnels through one shared God object. The fix is per-feature (or per-domain-concept) repositories — an `OrderRepository`, a `ProfileRepository` — each owned by the team or module that actually needs it, with genuinely shared concerns (auth tokens, a base network client) factored into a small, stable, deliberately-scoped shared module instead of one catch-all.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: business logic leaking into the UI layer
slides.markdown:
Under deadline pressure, it's the fastest path to put a business rule directly in a view model or even a view — "only show the discount banner if the cart total exceeds $50 and the user hasn't used a promo this month" ends up as an inline conditional in the screen's code, because that's where the immediate need is.

The cost shows up later: that rule can't be unit-tested without instantiating the whole UI layer, it can't be reused if a second screen needs the same rule, and it silently drifts out of sync with a similar rule someone else wrote independently elsewhere. The fix is a domain-layer use case (`shouldShowDiscountBanner(cart, user)`) the view model calls and simply renders the boolean result — testable in isolation, reusable, and a single place to fix when the business rule inevitably changes.

slides.sectionTitle: The senior nuance: architecture is a cost you pay to avoid a bigger cost later
slides.markdown:
A junior answer treats Clean Architecture and modularization as inherently correct, applied maximally everywhere. A senior answer treats every layer and module boundary as a **cost** — more files, more interfaces, more indirection to trace through when debugging — that's worth paying only when it prevents a larger cost: an untestable business rule, an accidental coupling between two features that shouldn't know about each other, a build time that's eating real engineering hours.

The question worth asking before adding a layer or splitting a module isn't 'is this the textbook-correct architecture,' it's 'what specific, concrete pain does this prevent, at this team's actual size and this app's actual growth rate.' Answering that concretely — not just citing the pattern by name — is what separates a candidate who's memorized Clean Architecture from one who's actually made this trade-off on a real team.
